cards.definitions: Let (X,ρ) be a nonempty separable metric space with its Borel σ-algebra. Let Y be a nonempty separable near-metric space with loss ℓ:Y×Y→[0,∞), symmetric, zero exactly on equal pairs, satisfying ℓ(a,c)≤C(ℓ(a,b)+ℓ(b,c)) for a fixed finite C, and 0<sup_{a,b}ℓ(a,b)<∞. Separability means a countable dense subset in the corresponding topology; measurable functions use the Borel structures. The input process (X_t)_{t≥1} is arbitrary, without independence or stationarity assumptions. Labels have the form Y_t=f*(X_t) for one fixed unknown measurable function f*:X→Y. A learning rule is a sequence of measurable functions h_t:(X×Y)^{t−1}×X→Y; its prediction at time t uses the labeled past and the current X_t, before Y_t is revealed. Strong universal consistency under a process means that, for every f*, T^{-1}Σ_{t=1}^T ℓ(h_t((X_s,Y_s)_{s<t},X_t),Y_t) tends to zero almost surely. The probability-one event may depend on f*. SUOL is the set of processes for which some one rule has this property for all measurable f*. An optimistically universal rule has it for every process in SUOL, without being told the process law. SMV consists of those processes such that, for each countable measurable partition (A_j)_{j≥1} of X, the number |{j: A_j∩{X₁,…,X_T}≠∅}| is o(T) almost surely; the null event may depend on the partition. No computational running-time or sample-rate bound is part of the question. The identically zero loss is a separate trivial case in which all processes are learnable.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative resolution is the published COLT 2022 theorem: an optimistically universal rule exists, and SUOL=SMV. Both the learner and the process characterization match the deterministic-target bounded-loss setting of the historical question. A theorem only for i.i.d. processes or for a selected target class would not have sufficed.

cards.title: Sample complexity of proper PAC learning
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved: can the extra log(1/ε) factor be removed from the worst-case proper PAC sample bound for every binary concept class? Equivalently, is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty finite concept class H of VC dimension d≥1 admits proper realizable PAC learning from at most ⌈C(d+ln(1/δ))/ε⌉ independent labeled examples, for every 0<ε<1/8 and 0<δ<1/100? The answer is no: some classes require Ω((d ln(1/ε)+ln(1/δ))/ε) examples from every proper learner, even when arbitrary computation and internal randomness are allowed.
cards.why: Separates the statistical cost of predicting accurately from the additional requirement of expressing the predictor within a prescribed class. The resolution shows that representation constraints alone can increase sample complexity, independently of running time.
cards.status_note: Read the original classical question, the October 2018 journal correction and COLT 2020 Theorem 11 with the finite-domain part of its Appendix C construction. Matched properness, arbitrary distributions, internal randomization and worst-case sample count. The finite hard class can depend on accuracy; no uniform asymptotic lower bound for every fixed finite class is claimed. The source’s suggested quantum task was removed rather than promoted to a new question.

cards.definitions:
Let X be any nonempty finite set and H⊆{0,1}^X a nonempty set of Boolean functions. The class is known to the learner. Its VC dimension d is the greatest size of a subset S⊆X for which every labeling S→{0,1} is the restriction of some h∈H. The source uses finite Boolean-string domains; any finite X can be encoded injectively in {0,1}ⁿ with all hypotheses extended by the same fixed label on unused strings, preserving the VC dimension and the lower-bound task on distributions supported on X.

An unknown target h* belongs to H. An arbitrary unknown distribution P on X generates m independent examples (X₁,h*(X₁)),…,(X_m,h*(X_m)), with each Xᵢ drawn from P. A proper learner is a possibly randomized rule that, given these examples and ε,δ, always returns a hypothesis ĥ∈H. It may depend on H,ε,δ, but not on P or h* except through the sample. Its internal randomness is independent of the examples. The requirement is Pr[P({x:ĥ(x)≠h*(x)})≤ε]≥1−δ for every P and every h*∈H, with probability over samples and learner randomness. There are no membership queries, quantum examples or additional unlabeled data. There is no time bound, no representation-efficiency requirement and no charge for evaluating hypotheses; only the number of independent labeled examples is counted.

For fixed H,ε,δ, M_prop(H,ε,δ) is the smallest integer m≥0 for which such a learner exists. A learner that uses at most m examples on every run can be viewed as using exactly m and ignoring unused examples, so this is a worst-case sample budget, not an expectation or a stopping-time average. Properness is required of all outputs. The learner need not be consistent with its observed sample; restricting to an arbitrary empirical-risk minimizer would be a narrower algorithm class and would not prove a lower bound against all proper learners. Output outside H is disallowed even when it predicts the target well.

The proposed constant C is independent of H, |X|, d, ε and δ. The classical upper bound O((d ln(1/ε)+ln(1/δ))/ε) has such universal constants. The later finite-domain lower bound states that a universal a>0 exists such that for each d≥1 and admissible ε,δ there is a finite class of VC dimension d with M_prop≥a(d ln(1/ε)+ln(1/δ))/ε. The class may depend on the accuracy; it is not asserted that one fixed finite class incurs the full logarithmic penalty as ε tends to zero. Theorem 11 supplies finite classes with arbitrarily large dual Helly number, and its Appendix C verifies the finite construction; choosing that auxiliary parameter sufficiently large gives the stated worst-class conclusion. Its additional infinite-class result is not needed to refute the universal finite-class bound. Logarithms here are natural; changing their base changes universal constants only.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical negative resolution requires a lower bound against every proper learner for some concept classes, not merely an example of a bad ERM rule. The published lower bound matches the general proper-learning upper bound in its d ln(1/ε) and ln(1/δ) terms and excludes a universal log-free bound. It does not say that all classes incur this penalty, nor that computational hardness is responsible.
